final_message:
All three versions are written, and each passes all 3 samples (s1, s2, s3) byte for byte, with LF line endings like the `.out` files.

I also wrote a slow, direct reference solver in `tools/` and checked against it on 7 edge-case grids: 1×1, a single row, no walls, an open cell walled in on all sides, S = 0, and random grids. All three versions match it on every case, and they give identical output on a 400×400×250 benchmark-size input.

**Algorithm (shared by all three):** I add a border of wall cells around the grid; one wall column is shared between neighbouring rows. Walls hold 0, so a wall neighbour adds nothing. Instead, each open cell gets a weight for its own value of 4 + k, where k is its number of wall neighbours, so `new = (weight·old + up + down + left + right) >> 3`. Sources and walls are restored or masked after each step. An open cell with walls on all four sides always stays 0, so it is skipped.

**Speed choices:**
- **`rust/src/main.rs`:** Values never go above 9000, so each cell is stored in 16 bits. That keeps the whole working set (~800 KB) inside the L2 cache. The weighted centre and the neighbour sum each fit in 16 bits; only their total can overflow, and the lost top bit is restored with an unsigned carry check. The update is branchless, and LLVM turns it into a 16-cells-at-a-time AVX2 loop. The program checks at runtime that the CPU supports AVX2 (standard library only, no build flags) and falls back to plain code otherwise. Release profile: `lto = "fat"`, `codegen-units = 1`, `panic = "abort"`.
  - One trap: when the select was written as an `if`, LLVM compiled it as a real per-element branch, which was about 6× slower. The mask-based select fixed that.
  - At 2,500 steps it runs at about 0.14 ns per cell update. The benchmark size takes about 0.12 s, almost all of which is process startup.
- **`plain.py`:** The whole grid is one Python big integer with a 17-bit slot per cell, so one big-int operation updates every cell at once. Slots never carry into each other because the per-cell total stays below 2¹⁷.
  - Each step is a few whole-grid big-int operations. One small multiplication covers left, right and the 4·centre term together; two shifts add the vertical neighbours. Two pre-built masks add the wall corrections, and a final shift, mask and OR finish the step.
  - The masks are built from the grid text using `translate` and string joins. The final values are read back from the binary string, and the totals are summed with built-in functions.
  - The benchmark size takes about 1.3 s wall time. About 0.45 s of that is Python startup and about 0.5 s is the simulation loop.
- **`fast.py`:** NumPy on int32 arrays with a flat layout. Each neighbour is just a shifted view of the array, so nothing is copied. There are 8 ufunc calls per step, all writing into buffers allocated once, and two arrays are swapped between steps.
  - I tried two other approaches; neither was faster: splitting the work into row chunks to fit the cache, and the 16-bit carry trick in NumPy.
  - The benchmark size takes about 0.9 s wall time, of which about 0.29 s is the actual work; the rest is starting Python and importing NumPy.

The machine was busy during testing, so these timings varied by roughly ±30%.

My test helpers (`tools/gen.py`, `tools/ref.py` and the test inputs) are in `tools/`; you can delete that folder.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
